title: Jussive and cohortative

objectives.can: Recognise the cohortative and the jussive and read them as wish, command or resolve.

explanation.summary: Besides the imperative, Hebrew has two prefix forms that express what the speaker wants: the cohortative for the 1st person ('let me', 'let us') and the jussive for the 3rd and 2nd persons ('let him', 'let there be', 'do not'). They often look like the yiqtol, and the corpus labels them case by case.

sections.heading: Three ways to express the will
body: When a speaker wants something done, Hebrew uses one of three forms. The imperative addresses a second person directly: פְּתַח, 'open!'. The cohortative is the speaker's own wish or resolve in the 1st person: 'let me go', 'let us build'. The jussive expresses a wish or command about a 3rd person, or, with אַל, a negative command to a 2nd person. Grammarians call all three volitive forms, forms of the will.

None of them is a tense. A speaker may be commanding, asking, offering, permitting or resolving, depending on who is speaking to whom. A king's jussive is an order; a petitioner's is a prayer. The form says what is wanted, and the situation says how.

sections.heading: The cohortative: first person with -ָה
body: The cohortative is a 1st person yiqtol, singular or plural, that takes the ending -ָה: אֵלְכָה, 'let me go', and נֵלְכָה, 'let us go'. In Ruth 2:2 the young woman says to Naomi that she will go to the field. In Genesis 11:3 the builders of Babel urge one another with נִלְבְּנָה, 'let us make bricks'. The ending is not a feminine ending; it is the mark of the will in the first person.

Most cohortatives in the corpus (about five in six) carry the ending -ָה, and a good number do not. Verbs that cannot take it show a plain yiqtol shape and are labelled cohortative from context, as in Genesis 11:4: נִבְנֶה and וְנַעֲשֶׂה, 'let us build', 'let us make'. Third-he verbs such as בָּנָה and עָשָׂה already end in -ֶה, and the edition still marks them cohortative when they express the wish.

sections.heading: The jussive: third and second person, short where it can be
body: The jussive is the prefix form of the 3rd person (and of the 2nd person after אַל). Where the verb allows it, the jussive is shortened. The same shortening as in the wayyiqtol: the third-he verb drops its ending. In Genesis 1:3 God says יְהִי אוֹר, 'let there be light', and the narrative continues וַיְהִי אוֹר, 'and there was light'. The first is the jussive, the second the wayyiqtol; both are short forms of הָיָה, and only the וַ and the sense tell them apart.

Many verbs have no short form: the regular strong verb has the same letters and vowels in the jussive as in the yiqtol. Then the corpus's label rests on the analysis of the edition it follows, and it is a decision about meaning rather than about shape. In Genesis 15:1, אַל תִּירָא is labelled a jussive, 'do not fear', although תִּירָא is spelled as a yiqtol would be. The same spelling of אֵלְכָה is labelled a cohortative in some verses and a yiqtol in others. A learner should read the form, the particle and the context, and not rely on a label alone.

sections.heading: אַל and נָא; what follows
body: The negative command to a 2nd person is usually אַל with the jussive. In Genesis 13:8 Abram says to Lot אַל נָא תְהִי מְרִיבָה, 'let there be no strife, please'. The particle נָא is a polite, urging word, 'please' or 'now': Abram is asking, not commanding. The jussive of הָיָה is תְהִי, in the 3rd feminine singular, agreeing with the noun מְרִיבָה.

A volitive form is often followed by another verb that states the purpose or the intended result. This is common usage, not a rule without exceptions. In Ruth 2:2 the cohortative אֵלְכָה, 'let me go', is followed by a second cohortative, וַאֲלַקֳטָּה, 'and let me glean'. In Exodus 7:16 God's command שַׁלַּח, 'let go!', is followed by וְיַעַבְדֻנִי, 'that they may serve me'. The second verb is a yiqtol in the corpus, and it is translated as a purpose. The commanding form sets the aim; the next verb tells what the aim is.

misunderstandings: The ending -ָה of the cohortative is not feminine, and it is not the directional ending that nouns take. On a 1st person verb it marks a wish or a resolve.
The jussive is not a past or future tense. It marks a wish, a command or a prohibition, and the time is that of the speech.

Do not expect every jussive or cohortative to look different from the yiqtol. Many look the same, and the label in the corpus follows the edition's analysis. Use the person, the particle אַל or נָא and the context.
A short form is not proof of a jussive. The wayyiqtol takes the same short shape in the same verbs. The וַ in front and a past narrative context mark the wayyiqtol.

deeper.heading: Why the labels differ
body: Grammarians have long noted that the cohortative and the jussive are visibly different from the yiqtol only in some verbs and persons. Most descriptions treat them as the same prefix conjugation used with a volitive meaning, with extra marks where the verb allows. The corpus follows the edition it was built from: in Psalm 113:2 the same word יְהִי that is jussive in Genesis 1:3 is labelled yiqtol. This lesson therefore teaches the shapes and the meanings, and leaves the label as a guide, not a proof.

examples.analysis: יְהִי is the Qal jussive 3rd masculine singular of הָיָה: 'let there be'. It is God's command. וַיְהִי is the wayyiqtol of the same verb: 'and there was'. The two forms are both short, and the וַ and the narrative sense separate the wish from the report.
